effund: To pour out. (old) Dr. H. More.
efflate: To fill with breath; to puff up. Sir T. Herbert.
effect: 1. Execution; performance; realization; operation; as, the law goes into effect in May. That no compunctious visitings of nature Shake my fell purpose, nor keep peace between The effect and it. Shak. | 1. To produce, as a cause or agent; to cause to be. So great a body such exploits to effect. Daniel. 2. To bring to pass; to execute; to enforce; to achieve; to accomplish.
efficient: Causing effects; producing results; that makes the effect to be what it is; actively operative; not inactive, slack, or incapable; characterized by energetic and useful activity; | An efficient cause; a prime mover. God . . . moveth mere natural agents as an efficient only. Hooker.
effront: To give assurance to. (old) Sir T. Browne.
effusion: 1. The act of pouring out; as, effusion of water, of blood, of grace, of words, and the like. To save the effusion of my people's blood. Dryden. 2. That which is poured out, literally or figuratively. Wash me with that precious effusion, and I shall be whiter than sow. Eikon Basilike. The light effusions of a heedless boy. Byron. 3.
efficacy: Power to produce effects; operation or energy of an agent or force; production of the effect intended; as, the efficacy of medicine in counteracting disease; the efficacy of prayer. "Of noxious efficacy." Milton. Syn. -- Virtue; force; energy; potency; efficiency.
effulge: To cause to shine with abundance of light; to radiate; to beam. His eyes effulging a peculiar fire. Thomson.
effective: Having the power to produce an effect or effects; producing a decided or decisive effect; efficient; serviceable; operative; as, an effective force, remedy, speech; the effective men in a regiment. | 1. That which produces a given effect; a cause. Jer. Taylor. 2. One who is capable of active service. He assembled his army -- 20,000 effectives -- at Corinth. W. P. Johnston. 3. Etym: [F.
efficience: 1. The quality of being efficient or producing an effect or effects; efficient power; effectual agency. The manner of this divine efficiency being far above us. Hooker. 2. (Mech.) The ratio of useful work to energy expended. Rankine. Efficiency of a heat engine, the ratio of the work done an engine, to the work due to the heat supplied to it.
effluviable: Capable of being given off as an effluvium. "Effluviable matter." Boyle.
effigiation: The act of forming in resemblance; an effigy. Fuller.
efflux: 1. The act or process of flowing out, or issuing forth; effusion; outflow; as, the efflux of matter from an ulcer; the efflux of men's piety. It is then that the devout affections . . . | To run out; to flow forth; to pass away. (old) Boyle.
effluent: Flowing out; as, effluent beams. Parnell. | A stream that flows out of another stream or lake.
effable: Capable of being uttered or explained; utterable. Barrow.
effeminate: 1. Having some characteristic of a woman, as delicacy, luxuriousness, etc.; soft or delicate to an unmanly degree; womanish; weak. The king, by his voluptuous life and mean marriage, became… | To make womanish; to make soft and delicate; to weaken. It will not corrupt or effeminate children's minds. Locke.
effulgent: Diffusing a flood of light; shining; luminous; beaming; bright; splendid. "Effulgent rays of light." Cowper.
effectuate: To bring to pass; to effect; to achieve; to accomplish; to fulfill. A fit instrument to effectuate his desire. Sir P. Sidney. In order to effectuate the thorough reform. G. T. Curtis.
eft: (a) A European lizard of the genus Seps. (b) A salamander, esp. the European smooth newt (Triton punctatus). | Again; afterwards; soon; quickly. (old) I wold never eft comen into the snare. Spenser.
efforce: To force; to constrain; to compel to yield. (old) Spenser.
efflation: The act of filling with wind; a breathing or puffing out; a puff, as of wind. A soft efflation of celestial fire. Parnell.
effectually: 1. With effect; efficaciously. 2. Actually; in effect. (old) Fuller.
effascination: A charming; state of being bewitched or deluded. (old)
efface: 1. To cause to disappear (as anything impresses or inscribed upon a surface) by rubbing out, striking out, etc.; to erase; to render illegible or indiscernible; as, to efface the letters on a monument, or the inscription on a coin. 2. To destroy, as a mental impression; to wear away. Efface from his mind the theories and notions vulgarly received. Bacon. Syn. -- To blot out;
effervesce: 1. To be in a state of natural ebullition; to bubble and hiss, as fermenting liquors, or any fluid, when some part escapes in a gaseous form. 2. To exhibit, in lively natural expression, feelings that can not be repressed or concealed; as, to effervesce with joy or merriment.
effervescency: A kind of natural ebullition; that commotion of a fluid which takes place when some part of the mass flies off in a gaseous form, producing innumerable small bubbles; as, the effervescence of a carbonate with citric acid.
effluence: 1. A flowing out, or emanation. 2. That which flows or issues from any body or substance; issue; efflux. Bright effluence of bright essence increate! Milton. And, as if the gloom of the earth and sky had been but the effluence of these two mortal hearts, it vanished with their sorrow. Hawthorne.
effete: No longer capable of producing young, as an animal, or fruit, as the earth; hence, worn out with age; exhausted of energy; incapable of efficient action; no longer productive; barren; sterile. Effete results from virile efforts. Mrs. Browning If they find the old governments effete, worn out, . . . they may seek new ones. Burke.
effort: 1. An exertion of strength or power, whether physical or mental, in performing an act or aiming at an object; more or less strenuous endeavor; struggle directed to the accomplishment of an object; | To stimulate. (old) "He efforted his spirits." Fuller.
efficiency: 1. The quality of being efficient or producing an effect or effects; efficient power; effectual agency. The manner of this divine efficiency being far above us. Hooker. 2. (Mech.) The ratio of useful work to energy expended. Rankine. Efficiency of a heat engine, the ratio of the work done an engine, to the work due to the heat supplied to it.
effet: The common newt; -- called also asker, eft, evat, and ewt.
effluvium: Subtile or invisible emanation; exhalation perceived by the sense of smell; especially, noisome or noxious exhalation; as, the effluvium from diseased or putrefying bodies, or from ill drainage.
efform: To form; to shape. (old) Efforming their words within their lips. Jer. Taylor.
effectual: Producing, or having adequate power or force to produce, an intended effect; adequate; efficient; operative; decisive. Shak. Effectual steps for the suppression of the rebellion. Macaulay. Effectual calling (Theol.), a doctrine concerning the work of the Holy Spirit in producing conviction of sin and acceptance of salvation by Christ, -- one of the five points of Calvinism.
efflower: To remove the epidermis of (a skin) with a concave knife, blunt in its middle part, -- as in making chamois leather.
effeminately: 1. In an effeminate or womanish manner; weakly; softly; delicately. "Proud and effeminately gay." Fawkes. 2. By means of a woman; by the power or art of a woman. "Effeminately vanquished." Milton.
efflorescent: 1. That effloresces, or is liable to effloresce on exposure; as, an efflorescent salt. 2. Covered with an efflorescence.
effuse: 1. Poured out freely; profuse. (old) So should our joy be very effuse. Barrow. 2. Disposed to pour out freely; prodigal. (old) Young. 3. (Bot.) Spreading loosely, especially on one side; | Effusion; loss. "Much effuse of blood." Shak.
efficacious: Possessing the quality of being effective; productive of, or powerful to produce, the effect intended; as, an efficacious law. Syn. -- See Effectual. -- Ef`fi*ca"cious*ly, adv. -- Ef`fi*ca"cious*ness, n.
eftsoons: Again; anew; a second time; at once; speedily. (old) And, if he fall from his capel [horse] eftsone. Chaucer. The champion stout eftsoons dismounted. Spenser.
effervescive: Tending to produce effervescence. "An effervescive force." Hickok.
effervescent: Gently boiling or bubbling, by means of the disengagement of gas
effeminacy: Characteristic quality of a woman, such as softness, luxuriousness, delicacy, or weakness, which is unbecoming a man; womanish delicacy or softness; -- used reproachfully of men. Milton.
effloresce: 1. To blossom forth. Carlyle. 2. (Chem.) To change on the surface, or throughout, to a whitish, mealy, or crystalline powder, from a gradual decomposition, esp. from the loss of water, on simple exposure to the air; as, Glauber's salts, and many others, effloresce. 3.
effectible: Capable of being done or achieved; practicable; feasible. Sir T. Browne.
efformation: The act of giving shape or form. (old) Ray.
efferent: (a) Conveying outward, or discharging; -- applied to certain blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves, etc. (b) Conveyed outward; as, efferent impulses, i. e., such as are conveyed by the motor or efferent nerves from the central nervous organ outwards; -- opposed to afferent.
efflorescency: The state or quality of being efflorescent; efflorescence.
effrontery: Impudence or boldness in confronting or in transgressing the bounds of duty or decorum; insulting presumptuousness; shameless boldness; barefaced assurance. Corruption lost nothing of its effrontery. Bancroft. Syn. -- Impudence; sauciness. See Impudence.
effendi: Master; sir; -- a title of a Turkish state official and man of learning, especially one learned in the law.
effluxion: 1. The act of flowing out; effusion. 2. That which flows out; effluvium; emanation. Some light effluxions from spirit to spirit. Bacon.
effacement: The act if effacing; also, the result of the act.
effusive: Pouring out; pouring forth freely. "Washed with the effusive wave." Pope. Effusive rocks (Geol.), volcanic rocks, in distinction from so-called intrusive, or plutonic, rocks. -- Ef*fu"sive*ly, adv. -- Ef*fu"sive*ness, n.
effectless: Without effect or advantage; useless; bootless. Shak. -- Ef*fect"less*ly, adv.
effervescence: A kind of natural ebullition; that commotion of a fluid which takes place when some part of the mass flies off in a gaseous form, producing innumerable small bubbles; as, the effervescence of a carbonate with citric acid.
effume: To breathe or puff out. (old) B. Jonson.
eftsoon: Again; anew; a second time; at once; speedily. (old) And, if he fall from his capel [horse] eftsone. Chaucer. The champion stout eftsoons dismounted. Spenser.
effeminateness: The state of being effeminate; unmanly softness. Fuller.
effigy: The image, likeness, or representation of a person, whether a full figure, or a part; an imitative figure; -- commonly applied to sculptured likenesses, as those on monuments, or to those of the heads of princes on coins and medals, sometimes applied to portraits. To burn, or To hang, in effigy, to burn or to hang an image or picture of a person, as a token of public odium.
effulgence: The state of being effulgent; extreme brilliancy; a flood of light; great luster or brightness; splendor. The effulgence of his glory abides. Milton. The bright and the balmy effulgence of morn. Beattie.
effigiate: To form as an effigy; hence, to fashion; to adapt. [He must] effigiate and conform himself to those circumstances. Jer. Taylor.
effection: Creation; a doing. Sir M. Hale.
effossion: A digging out or up. "The effossion of coins." Arbuthnot.
effumability: The capability of flying off in fumes or vapor. (old) Boyle.
efflorescence: 1. (Bot.) Flowering, or state of flowering; the blooming of flowers; blowth. 2. (Med.) A redness of the skin; eruption, as in rash, measles, smallpox, scarlatina, etc. 3. (Chem.) (a) The formation of the whitish powder or crust on the surface of efflorescing bodies, as salts, etc. (b) The powder or crust thus formed.
effluviate: To give forth effluvium. "An effluviating power." Boyle.
